title: queues pub sub RabbitMQ Kafka ordering and delivery semantics
concepts: A broker mediates between publishers and consumers, but products called message brokers may implement different models: routed transient work queues, durable append-only logs, or both. Learn each product's contract instead of assuming the name queue or topic guarantees behavior.

Delivery is an end-to-end chain with distinct publisher acceptance, broker persistence or replication, consumer delivery, application processing, and acknowledgement points. A publisher confirm does not confirm consumer processing, and a consumer acknowledgement does not prove an external side effect is atomic.

At-least-once delivery allows duplicates, so consumers must make effects idempotent or deduplicate. At-most-once can lose work; exactly-once claims are scoped to a defined transactional boundary and do not automatically cover arbitrary external systems.

Ordering is scoped: a RabbitMQ queue has an enqueue order that can be affected by multiple consumers, priorities, requeueing, and redelivery; Kafka guarantees record order within a partition, not a total order across all partitions.

RabbitMQ routes each published message through an exchange and bindings to queues or streams; Kafka appends records to topic partitions and lets independent consumer groups track their own offsets. These are different routing and consumption models, not interchangeable labels.

Durability and availability consume resources and impose latency or operational tradeoffs. Select queue type, replication, retention, acknowledgement policy, and replay behavior from recovery requirements and verify them with failure tests.

RabbitMQ documents quorum queues and streams as its replicated data structures; classic queue mirroring was removed starting in RabbitMQ 4.0.
Quorum queues support delayed retry, delivery limits, and optional at-least-once dead-lettering; do not treat those guarantees as default for every queue type or DLX configuration.
Current queue docs state transient non-exclusive classic queues are deprecated and disabled by default beginning in RabbitMQ 4.3.0; this transition matters when upgrading from RabbitMQ 4.2.
Use current Kafka 4.4 documentation for broker, topic/partition, consumer-group, producer, offset, and processing-semantics terminology; exact client defaults and APIs remain client-version-specific.
